overview: The map’s two entries from 1000 to 1200 represent the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, a Deccan dynasty established by Taila II around 973. They are distinct from the earlier Chalukyas of Badami. Kalyani, today Basavakalyan, became their political center. The imported outlines are coarse snapshots, not frontiers that stayed fixed for two centuries; the map endpoints are not the dynasty’s beginning or end.

periods.title: Early Western Chalukya power
periods.summary: Satyashraya and then Jayasimha II ruled amid competition with the Cholas.

periods.title: Someshvara and contested succession
periods.summary: Someshvara I and his successors struggled over southern campaigns and the throne.

periods.title: Vikramaditya VI’s new era
periods.summary: Vikramaditya VI introduced an era counted from his accession in 1076.

periods.title: Later rule, displacement and restoration
periods.summary: Kalachuri rulers displaced Western Chalukya authority in the twelfth century; Someshvara IV briefly restored it before Yadava and Hoysala expansion.

items.text: A Dambal inscription dated 1095 to 1096 names Queen Lakshmadevi governing the Eighteen Agraharas and the city of Dharmapura, identified with Dambal. Its praise is ceremonial, but the administrative role is specific: a royal woman appears as a regional governor.

The same record credits sixteen merchants of Dambal with building a Buddhist vihara, and Sangavayya of Lakkundi with a second foundation dedicated to Tara. These were named townspeople financing religious institutions, alongside the royal government described above them.

The Dambal endowment assigned levies on bags traveling to and from the south to its two Buddhist establishments. Passing trade could therefore support worship and upkeep. The edition cannot confidently identify some commodities, so we cannot turn those bags into a precise shopping list.

At Lakkundi, the noblewoman Attimabbe sponsored the Brahma Jinalaya in 1007. She was the wife of Nagadeva and a major Jain patron. The building makes her contribution visible in stone: women could commission institutions remembered long after the rulers whose dates organize our timelines.

Attimabbe also supported Kannada literature, including the poet Ranna. She is celebrated for distributing a thousand copies of Ponna’s Shantipurana. These were handwritten manuscripts: supporting a book meant paying for the work of copying it, not pressing a print button.

A Kannada inscription at Nagai dated 1058 describes a school with 200 students of the Veda and 52 studying other established disciplines. This was a Brahman teaching institution, not universal schooling. Its unusually detailed endowment lets us count an actual scholarly community.

Nagai’s school employed six librarians alongside nine teachers. Each librarian received thirty mattars of land as remuneration. Keeping a manuscript collection working was a recognized job, supported by agricultural property rather than a modern monthly bank transfer.

The school’s bell-ringer received the same land allowance as each librarian and the commentator teaching logic. Other senior scholars received larger plots. Remembering when to assemble mattered enough to appear beside scholarship in the institution’s financial arrangements.

Nagai’s endowment also covered food and accommodation for scholars and students, including the librarians. Teaching required lodging and meals as well as learned books. The inscription’s budget preserves that practical side of keeping a school alive.

A 1008 grant from the Konkan chief Ratta Raja assigned the village of Krishnamandi to Avveshvara’s temple to support meals for ascetics, learned people and visitors. The donor was a tributary ruler within the Chalukya political world. A religious endowment could also feed travelers.

Chavundaraya II’s Lokopakara, composed in Kannada in 1025, assembled practical knowledge about subjects including cookery, perfumes, plants, animal medicine and building. It shows that learned writing could concern kitchens and the care of animals as well as royal victories. Its medical material records historical ideas, not tested modern treatments.

Lokopakara’s eighth chapter gives cookery in fifty-seven verses. Its instructions discuss ingredients and techniques without precise measurements or cooking times. A reader still needed experience: the manuscript was not going to beep when dinner was ready. These prescriptions cannot tell us what every family ate.

Lakkundi’s builders worked chloritic schist, using smaller blocks than the sandstone familiar from earlier Badami monuments. They filled temple surfaces with miniature towers, niches, pilasters and cornices. Choosing stone and carving intricate detail were practical achievements of workshops, not simply ideas in a royal order.

Look closely at Lakkundi’s sculpture and grand architecture becomes a collection of small discoveries: a griffin at the Jain temple and a horseman at Kashi Vishveshvara. The surviving carvings show how makers combined sacred buildings with lively animal and human figures.

Medieval Lakkundi’s surviving water architecture includes stepwells, particularly Musukina Bhavi beside Manikeshwar Temple. Steps made the water accessible below ground level. The heritage description does not supply an exact construction year, so this is a regional example rather than an event dated to a particular king.

sections.title: A few words from the period

items.text: “Namo Buddhāya” means “Reverence to Buddha!” This Sanskrit opening comes from the Dambal inscription of 1095 to 1096, which also contains Old Kannada. The sample uses normalized Roman transliteration of the published reading; the stone’s letters belong to the contemporary Kannada script tradition.

ending.text: The dynasty continued beyond the map’s first boundary in 1100. Kalachuri rulers displaced its authority in the twelfth century; Someshvara IV briefly restored it before Yadava and Hoysala expansion ended its wider power. Kannada literary, religious and craft traditions continued under changing rulers.
